questions.question: Why does Lear disown Cordelia during the division of his kingdom?

options.text: She refuses to flatter him beyond her honest duty.
She asks him to surrender his hundred knights.
She accuses Gloucester of plotting against him.
She chooses Edmund as her husband.

questions.explanation: Cordelia speaks of the love her bond requires; Lear treats her plainness as rejection.

evidence.exact:
CORDELIA.
Unhappy that I am, I cannot heave
My heart into my mouth: I love your majesty
According to my bond; no more nor less.

LEAR.
Let it be so, thy truth then be thy dower:
For, by the sacred radiance of the sun,
The mysteries of Hecate and the night;
By all the operation of the orbs,
From whom we do exist and cease to be;
Here I disclaim all my paternal care,
Propinquity and property of blood,
And as a stranger to my heart and me
Hold thee from this for ever. The barbarous Scythian,
Or he that makes his generation messes
To gorge his appetite, shall to my bosom
Be as well neighbour’d, pitied, and reliev’d,
As thou my sometime daughter.

questions.question: Why does the banished Kent return in disguise?

options.text: To help Edmund acquire Edgar’s inheritance.
To continue serving Lear without being recognized.
To persuade Cordelia to abandon the French army.
To arrange a marriage between Goneril and Edmund.

questions.explanation: Kent changes his appearance and voice so he can still serve the master he loves.

evidence.exact:
KENT.
If but as well I other accents borrow,
That can my speech defuse, my good intent
May carry through itself to that full issue
For which I rais’d my likeness. Now, banish’d Kent,
If thou canst serve where thou dost stand condemn’d,
So may it come, thy master, whom thou lov’st,
Shall find thee full of labours.

questions.question: What is Edmund’s stated aim in his opening plot against Edgar?

options.text: To restore Cordelia’s lost share of the kingdom.
To prevent Gloucester from helping Lear.
To take the land reserved for his legitimate brother.
To preserve Edgar’s inheritance from Cornwall.

questions.explanation: Edmund resents the disadvantage of his birth and declares that he must have Edgar’s land.

evidence.exact:
EDMUND.
Thou, Nature, art my goddess; to thy law
My services are bound. Wherefore should I
Stand in the plague of custom, and permit
The curiosity of nations to deprive me?
For that I am some twelve or fourteen moonshines
Lag of a brother? Why bastard? Wherefore base?
When my dimensions are as well compact,
My mind as generous, and my shape as true
As honest madam’s issue? Why brand they us
With base? With baseness? bastardy? Base, base?
Who, in the lusty stealth of nature, take
More composition and fierce quality
Than doth within a dull stale tired bed
Go to the creating a whole tribe of fops
Got ’tween asleep and wake? Well then,
Legitimate Edgar, I must have your land:
Our father’s love is to the bastard Edmund
As to the legitimate: fine word: legitimate!
Well, my legitimate, if this letter speed,
And my invention thrive, Edmund the base
Shall top the legitimate. I grow, I prosper.
Now, gods, stand up for bastards!

questions.question: Why does Edgar adopt the identity of Poor Tom?

options.text: To qualify as one of Lear’s hundred knights.
To collect a dowry from the King of France.
To conceal his service as Edmund’s messenger.
To escape capture by appearing to be a destitute beggar.

questions.explanation: Hunted as a proclaimed fugitive, Edgar disguises himself in the lowest and poorest shape he can imagine.

evidence.exact:
EDGAR.
I heard myself proclaim’d,
And by the happy hollow of a tree
Escap’d the hunt. No port is free, no place
That guard and most unusual vigilance
Does not attend my taking. While I may scape
I will preserve myself: and am bethought
To take the basest and most poorest shape
That ever penury in contempt of man,
Brought near to beast: my face I’ll grime with filth,
Blanket my loins; elf all my hair in knots,
And with presented nakedness outface
The winds and persecutions of the sky.
The country gives me proof and precedent
Of Bedlam beggars, who, with roaring voices,
Strike in their numb’d and mortified bare arms
Pins, wooden pricks, nails, sprigs of rosemary;
And with this horrible object, from low farms,
Poor pelting villages, sheep-cotes, and mills,
Sometime with lunatic bans, sometime with prayers,
Enforce their charity. Poor Turlygod! poor Tom,
That’s something yet: Edgar I nothing am.

questions.question: What issue brings Lear into renewed conflict with both Goneril and Regan before the storm?

options.text: Their demands that he reduce or surrender his attendants.
Their refusal to allow Cordelia to marry France.
Their wish to make Edgar heir to Gloucester.
Their decision to send Kent into battle at Dover.

questions.explanation: The sisters progressively question the number and need of Lear’s followers, which he sees as an attack on his dignity.

evidence.exact:
REGAN.
Why not, my lord? If then they chanc’d to slack ye,
We could control them. If you will come to me,—
For now I spy a danger,—I entreat you
To bring but five-and-twenty: to no more
Will I give place or notice.
evidence.suffix:
LEAR.
I gave you all,—

REGAN.

evidence.suffix:

O, reason not the need:

evidence.exact:
LEAR.
O, reason not the need: our basest beggars
Are in the poorest thing superfluous:
Allow not nature more than nature needs,
Man’s life is cheap as beast’s. Thou art a lady;
If only to go warm were gorgeous,
Why, nature needs not what thou gorgeous wear’st
Which scarcely keeps thee warm. But, for true need,—
You heavens, give me that patience, patience I need!
You see me here, you gods, a poor old man,
As full of grief as age; wretched in both!
If it be you that stirs these daughters’ hearts
Against their father, fool me not so much
To bear it tamely; touch me with noble anger,
And let not women’s weapons, water-drops,
Stain my man’s cheeks! No, you unnatural hags,
I will have such revenges on you both
That all the world shall,—I will do such things,—
What they are yet, I know not; but they shall be
The terrors of the earth. You think I’ll weep;
No, I’ll not weep:— [Storm and tempest.]
I have full cause of weeping; but this heart
Shall break into a hundred thousand flaws
Or ere I’ll weep.—O fool, I shall go mad!

questions.question: Why has Gloucester sent Lear to Dover when Cornwall and Regan interrogate him?

options.text: To deliver Lear to Edmund as a prisoner.
To protect Lear from his daughters’ cruelty.
To have Lear restore Cornwall’s lost title.
To stop Lear from meeting the French forces.

questions.explanation: Gloucester says he wanted to spare Lear further cruelty from Regan and her sister.

evidence.exact:
CORNWALL.
Where hast thou sent the King?

GLOUCESTER.
To Dover.

REGAN.
Wherefore to Dover? Wast thou not charg’d at peril,—

CORNWALL.
Wherefore to Dover? Let him first answer that.

GLOUCESTER.
I am tied to the stake, and I must stand the course.

REGAN.
Wherefore to Dover, sir?

GLOUCESTER.
Because I would not see thy cruel nails
Pluck out his poor old eyes; nor thy fierce sister
In his anointed flesh stick boarish fangs.
The sea, with such a storm as his bare head
In hell-black night endur’d, would have buoy’d up,
And quench’d the stelled fires;
Yet, poor old heart, he holp the heavens to rain.
If wolves had at thy gate howl’d that stern time,
Thou shouldst have said, ‘Good porter, turn the key.’
All cruels else subscrib’d: but I shall see
The winged vengeance overtake such children.

questions.question: What is Edgar’s purpose in pretending to guide Gloucester to a fatal cliff?

options.text: To help Gloucester carry out his wish to die.
To persuade Gloucester that Edmund is innocent.
To cure Gloucester’s despair through a staged survival.
To lead Gloucester into Cornwall’s custody.

questions.explanation: Edgar explicitly says that his deception is intended to cure his father’s despair.

evidence.exact:
EDGAR.
[Aside.] Why I do trifle thus with his despair
Is done to cure it.

options.text: She demands that he return her former dowry.
She sends him back to live with Goneril.
She asks Edmund to judge his conduct.
She denies that she has cause to hate him.

questions.question: What does the dying Edmund try to revoke?

options.text: His order to kill Lear and Cordelia.
Lear’s decree banishing Kent.
Gloucester’s decision to disinherit Edgar.
Cornwall’s order to put Kent in the stocks.

questions.explanation: Edmund sends an urgent warning because his writ threatens the lives of Lear and Cordelia.

questions.question: What is the outcome for Lear and Cordelia at the end?

options.text: Cordelia survives to rule jointly with Lear.
Cordelia is dead, and Lear dies grieving over her.
Lear dies while Cordelia departs with France.
Lear survives and sends Cordelia back to prison.

questions.explanation: Lear enters carrying Cordelia’s body and dies after lamenting that she has no breath.

evidence.exact: Enter Lear with Cordelia dead in his arms; Edgar, Officer and others following.

LEAR.
And my poor fool is hang’d! No, no, no life!
Why should a dog, a horse, a rat have life,
And thou no breath at all? Thou’lt come no more,
Never, never, never, never, never!
Pray you undo this button. Thank you, sir.
Do you see this? Look on her: look, her lips,
Look there, look there!

[He dies.]
